pos: n. (the midland Anglo-Saxon kingdom, last of the English realms to be converted, and supreme in England in the eighth century)
etymology: Latinised from Old English Mierce, the borderers or march people, from mearc, a boundary.
biblical_def: Mercia was the kingdom of the English midlands, named from the border people, and it was the last of the great English realms to receive the gospel. Penda, who ruled it from about 626 to 655, was the most formidable heathen king in English history: he killed Edwin and Oswald of Northumbria and Sigebert and Anna of East Anglia in battle, and he died fighting Oswiu at the Winwaed. He did not persecute Christians, and Bede notes that he allowed preachers in his kingdom and despised only converts who did not keep the faith they professed. His son Peada was baptised before his death, his sons Wulfhere and Ethelred were Christian, Chad was given Lichfield as his see, and under Offa in the later eighth century Mercia dominated England and briefly had an archbishopric of its own at Lichfield. The dictionary records Mercia because Penda is the clearest English case of a ruler who is no friend of the church and whom God nevertheless uses. Scripture insists on this repeatedly: the king's heart is in the LORD'S hand, Nebuchadnezzar is called his servant, Assyria is the rod of his anger, and the powers that be are ordained of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a king as a chief ruler; a heart as the seat of the will and affections; a rod as an instrument of correction; a power as one invested with authority; and to ordain as to appoint and establish.
webster_full: KING, n. The chief or sovereign of a nation; a man invested with supreme authority over a nation, tribe or country.
HEART, n. The seat of the affections and passions; the will; the seat of understanding and of purpose.
ROD, n. The instrument of punishment or correction; hence, punishment or chastisement; also, a staff of authority.
POWER, n. Command; the right of governing; one who is invested with authority; a ruling magistrate or state.
ORDAIN, v.t. To appoint; to decree; to establish; to institute; to set in order.
corruption_summary: The midland Anglo-Saxon kingdom of the border people, held by the heathen Penda until 655 and supreme in England under Offa.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God governs rulers who do not acknowledge him. Solomon states the mechanism without qualification: “The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will” (Pro 21:1). Jeremiah is made to call a pagan conqueror by a startling title, “Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant” (Jer 27:6).

The live temptation is to read political history as though the church's fortunes depended on having friendly kings. Penda was not friendly and the gospel entered his kingdom anyway; Offa was baptised and used the church as an instrument of his power. Isaiah addresses an empire that had no idea whose purposes it served, “O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger” (Isa 10:5). Paul draws the practical conclusion for Christians under any government whatever, in a letter written while Nero reigned: “For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1).

pos: n. (the kingdom of the West Saxons, which outlasted every rival and became the kingdom of England)
etymology: Latinised from Old English West Seaxe, the West Saxons; the modern form was revived by antiquaries.
biblical_def: Wessex was the kingdom of the West Saxons, founded, the Chronicle says, by Cerdic in 495, and the one English kingdom that survived everything. Birinus preached to its king Cynegils about 635 and set his see at Dorchester on Thames, later moved to Winchester; Aldhelm and then Boniface came out of its monasteries; Ine issued the earliest surviving West Saxon laws about 694, with clauses on baptism, Sunday work and church dues. Egbert made it the chief English kingdom in 825, and when the Danes had destroyed Northumbria, Mercia and East Anglia, Alfred held Wessex alone, bought time at Athelney, won at Edington in 878, and then set about translating books into English because he thought the collapse had come from ignorance. His house went on to rule all England. The dictionary records Wessex because its survival was not a matter of resources, which it did not have in 878, nor of probability. Scripture ascribes the frustration of great plans and the standing of God's own purpose to the same hand: the counsel of the heathen comes to nothing, the counsel of the LORD stands for ever.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines counsel as deliberation and advice; a device as a contrived plan; to purpose as to intend; to direct as to point out a course; and a thought as an intention or design.
webster_full: COUNSEL, n. Advice; opinion given for directing the judgment or conduct of another; deliberation; consultation.
DEVICE, n. That which is formed by design; a contrivance; an invention; a scheme formed in the mind; a stratagem.
PURPOSE, v.t. To intend; to design; to resolve; to determine on some end or object to be accomplished.
DIRECT, v.t. To point out a course to; to guide; to show the right road or course; to regulate.
THOUGHT, n. The operation of the mind; idea; conception; design; purpose; opinion.
corruption_summary: The kingdom of the West Saxons, converted under Cynegils, which alone survived the Danish conquests and under Alfred's house became England.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the asymmetry between human plans and God's. The Psalmist puts the two in parallel so that the contrast is unmistakable: “The LORD bringeth the counsel of the heathen to nought” (Psa 33:10), while “The counsel of the LORD standeth for ever, the thoughts of his heart to all generations” (Psa 33:11). Wessex in the winter of 878 had nothing else to appeal to.

The live temptation, especially in an English-speaking country with a long Christian history, is to convert this into national flattery, as though Alfred's survival were a promise made to a people. The oath in Isaiah is given about God's purpose and not about anyone's nation: “Surely as I have thought, so shall it come to pass; and as I have purposed, so shall it stand” (Isa 14:24). What is left to men is the planning and the walking, with the outcome withheld: “A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps” (Pro 16:9). Alfred devised a great deal, and he also had the marshes.

pos: n. (the south-eastern English kingdom, the first to receive the gospel, where Augustine landed in 597)
etymology: From British Cantium, perhaps the border or the coastal land; Old English Cent.
biblical_def: Kent was the first English kingdom to be Christianised, because it was the nearest to the Continent and because its king had married a Christian. Ethelbert's Frankish queen Bertha brought her chaplain Liudhard with her and worshipped in a surviving Roman church at Canterbury; Gregory the Great sent Augustine with forty companions in 596, they landed on Thanet in 597, and the king gave them leave to preach, saying he could not abandon the beliefs of his people but would not forbid them. He was baptised within the year, and Bede records that he compelled no one, having learned that the service of Christ must be voluntary. Kent afterwards produced the first written English laws, the first English cathedral and the primatial see. The dictionary records Kent for Ethelbert's restraint. The gospel entered England by preaching and persuasion and not by a royal decree, and that is the scriptural pattern: Joshua puts a choice before the people, Samuel calls them to return with all their hearts, and Paul is sent to open men's eyes rather than to bind their hands.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to choose as to select by preference; to serve as to work for and obey; to return as to come back; to turn as to change direction; and to worship as to adore with reverence.
webster_full: CHOOSE, v.t. To pick out; to select; to take by way of preference from two or more things offered; to elect.
SERVE, v.t. To work for; to bestow the labor of body and mind in the employment of another; to obey and worship.
RETURN, v.i. To come or go back; to come to the same place or state; to revert; to come again.
TURN, v.t. To cause to move in a circular course; to change from one state or course to another; to convert.
WORSHIP, v.t. To adore; to pay divine honors to; to reverence with supreme respect and veneration.
corruption_summary: The first Christian English kingdom, where Bertha's chapel preceded Augustine's landing in 597 and Ethelbert refused to compel his people.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that conversion is persuaded and not legislated. Joshua lays the matter before Israel as a choice and then commits only himself and his household: “choose you this day whom ye will serve” (Jos 24:15). Samuel calls for a turning that is internal before it is outward, “If ye do return unto the LORD with all your hearts, then put away the strange gods” (1Sa 7:3).

The live temptation, soon realised in English history, is the king's religion imposed on the king's subjects, which Ethelbert declined and his successors did not. Paul's commission describes the actual work and the actual agent: he is sent “To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light” (Act 26:18), which is a thing done by a word to a mind. The end in view is a worship that is willingly given by every nation: “All nations whom thou hast made shall come and worship before thee, O Lord” (Psa 86:9), and a compelled worship is not that.

pos: n. (the southern of the two Northumbrian kingdoms, centred on York and the Yorkshire wolds)
etymology: From a British name, perhaps deifr, waters, latinised by Bede as Deira.
biblical_def: Deira was the southern half of Northumbria, the country between the Humber and the Tees with its centre at York, and it was politically distinct from Bernicia to the north for most of the seventh century. Edwin of Deira was baptised at York in 627 by Paulinus and gave the church its first northern see; after Edwin fell to Penda and Cadwallon the kingdom passed under Bernician control, and its last separate king, Oswin, was murdered in 651 at the instigation of Oswiu and buried at Tynemouth. Deira then ceased to exist as a kingdom, though the name survived in Yorkshire place names and in the title of its bishops. The dictionary records Deira because it is a kingdom that vanished within a century of hearing the gospel, which is an ordinary fate for kingdoms and no measure at all of what was done in it. Scripture is content to say that every realm will change hands at last, that the God of heaven will set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, and that the righteous man rather than the dynasty is the everlasting foundation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a kingdom as the territory of a king; to reign as to possess sovereign power; to destroy as to demolish or ruin; a foundation as the basis of a building; and remembrance as the keeping in mind.
webster_full: KINGDOM, n. The territory or country subject to a king; dominion; rule; sovereign power.
REIGN, v.i. To possess or exercise sovereign power or authority; to rule; to be predominant.
DESTROY, v.t. To demolish; to pull down; to ruin; to annihilate a thing by demolishing or by burning.
FOUNDATION, n. The basis of an edifice; the ground work of any thing; that on which any thing stands.
REMEMBRANCE, n. The retaining or having in mind the idea of a thing which had before been known; honorable memory.
corruption_summary: The southern Northumbrian kingdom, centred on York, Christianised under Edwin in 627 and extinguished as a separate realm by 651.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one that makes the extinction of a kingdom bearable: all of them change hands. John hears it announced as a finished fact: “The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ” (Rev 11:15). Daniel had already distinguished the one realm that is not provisional: “And in the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed” (Dan 2:44).

The live temptation when a people disappears is to conclude that its work disappeared too. Deira lasted barely a generation after Edwin's baptism and gave the north its first bishop, its first stone church and Hild's generation of abbesses. Solomon marks the difference between what the storm takes and what it leaves: “As the whirlwind passeth, so is the wicked no more: but the righteous is an everlasting foundation” (Pro 10:25). The Psalter promises the same permanence to persons rather than to realms: “the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance” (Psa 112:6).

pos: n. (the northern Northumbrian kingdom from the Tees to the Forth, with its fortress at Bamburgh)
etymology: From a British name, perhaps Bryneich, the land of the passes, latinised by Bede as Bernicia.
biblical_def: Bernicia was the northern half of Northumbria, running from the Tees to the Firth of Forth, with its royal fortress on the basalt rock at Bamburgh above the sea and Lindisfarne in sight of it. Its kings were the dominant English house of the seventh century: Ethelfrith, then Edwin's rival Oswald, who had been baptised in exile among the Scots and who sent to Iona for Aidan in 635, then Oswiu, who settled the Easter question at Whitby in 664. Oswald set up a wooden cross before the battle of Heavenfield and prayed with his army, and Bede makes his reign the beginning of the northern church. The fortress rock and the tidal island together are the geography of the whole story: a king on a crag and a bishop on an island, three miles apart. The dictionary records Bernicia for the figure its fortress supplies. Scripture uses the shelter of a rock and a stronghold constantly for God himself, and it is careful to say that the refuge is a person and not a position, the eternal God and his everlasting arms.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a refuge as shelter from danger; a fortress as a fortified place; a shadow as shade from the sun; to abide as to dwell; and everlasting as lasting for ever.
webster_full: REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects from danger, distress or calamity.
FORTRESS, n. A fortified place; a large and permanent fortification, sometimes including a town; a fort; a castle.
SHADOW, n. Shade within defined limits; obscurity or deprivation of light; shelter; protection.
ABIDE, v.i. To rest or dwell; to tarry or stay; to continue permanently or in the same state.
EVERLASTING, a. Lasting or enduring for ever; eternal; immortal; perpetual.
corruption_summary: The northern Northumbrian kingdom from the Tees to the Forth, with its fortress at Bamburgh, whose king Oswald sent to Iona for Aidan in 635.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the refuge Scripture promises is a person. The Psalmist uses exactly the imagery of a Bamburgh: “For thou hast been a shelter for me, and a strong tower from the enemy” (Psa 61:3), and then locates the safety in a dwelling rather than a wall, “He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty” (Psa 91:1).

The live temptation for a warrior kingdom is to confuse the figure with the fortification, and Bernicia's history shows how little the rock could do: Penda besieged Bamburgh and tried to burn it, and the kings of that house died one after another in battle. The Psalmist makes the confession personal and names the object: “I will say of the LORD, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust” (Psa 91:2). Moses's blessing says the same of a people with no fortress at all, “The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms” (Deu 33:27).

pos: n. (the kingdom and later province between the Humber and the Witham, where Paulinus baptised in the Trent)
etymology: Old English Lindeség, the island of Lindum, from the Roman name of Lincoln and eg, an island.
biblical_def: Lindsey was the low country between the Humber, the Trent and the Witham, nearly surrounded by water and fen, and in the seventh century it was a small kingdom disputed between Northumbria and Mercia. Paulinus preached there and baptised great numbers in the Trent at Littleborough, as Bede records on the word of an old man who had seen it; a see was set up at Sidnacester and the diocese later merged into Lincoln. Lindsey had no dynasty of its own after the eighth century and became an administrative division, one of the three parts of Lincolnshire. Its fens were drained in stages from the seventeenth century and became some of the best farmland in England. The dictionary records Lindsey for the fen. Scripture's standing promise about waste ground is not that it will be admired but that it will be changed: the wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad, rivers will be opened in high places, and the land that was desolate becomes like the garden of Eden. That is said of people before it is said of soil.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a wilderness as a desert or uncultivated tract; a desert as a waste region; to blossom as to put forth flowers; desolate as laid waste; and a garden as a piece of ground for plants.
webster_full: WILDERNESS, n. A desert; a tract of land or region uncultivated and uninhabited by human beings, whether a forest or a wide barren plain.
DESERT, n. An uninhabited tract of land; a region in its natural state; a wilderness; a solitude.
BLOSSOM, v.i. To put forth blossoms or flowers; to bloom; to blow; to flourish and prosper.
DESOLATE, a. Destitute or deprived of inhabitants; laid waste; in a ruinous condition; solitary.
GARDEN, n. A piece of ground appropriated to the cultivation of herbs or plants, fruits and flowers.
corruption_summary: The fenland kingdom between Humber, Trent and Witham, where Paulinus baptised in the Trent, later absorbed into Mercia and the diocese of Lincoln.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's promises about waste ground are promises of change. Isaiah does not say the desert will be endured: “the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose” (Isa 35:1), and the means is water brought where there was none, “I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water” (Isa 41:18).

The live temptation is to read such passages as agricultural optimism, as though the point were drainage. The prophets apply the figure to a people restored: the saying put in the mouths of onlookers is about a nation, “This land that was desolate is become like the garden of Eden” (Eze 36:35), and Isaiah makes the comfort of Zion the subject and the garden the comparison, “he will comfort all her waste places; and he will make her wilderness like Eden” (Isa 51:3). A fen kingdom whose people were baptised in a river had both halves of the picture in front of it.

pos: n. (the British kingdom in the Yorkshire hills that survived among the English until about 617)
etymology: From a British name of uncertain sense, surviving in Barwick in Elmet and Sherburn in Elmet.
biblical_def: Elmet was a British kingdom in the hills and woods of what is now west Yorkshire, between the Pennines and the Vale of York, and it held out as a British realm inside English territory until Edwin of Northumbria expelled its king Ceretic about 617. It is remembered in the names of villages that still carry it, and it is the reason there was a British Christian population in the area before the English conversion, since the British church survived in such pockets while the English round them were heathen. Nothing of its own records remains. The dictionary records Elmet for the shape of the thing: a small Christian people in the hills, surrounded, not expanding, finally absorbed, and faithful in the meantime. Scripture has no contempt for that position. God promises a remnant that escapes the sword, he calls a man a hiding place and a shadow of a great rock in a weary land, and Habakkuk works out in the plainest terms how to rejoice when the fig tree does not blossom and the fields yield no meat.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a covert as a shelter or hiding place; a remnant as that which is left; to escape as to get free from danger; a blast as a gust of wind; and to rejoice as to be glad.
webster_full: COVERT, n. A covering, shelter or defence; a thicket; a hiding place; a shelter from the weather.
REMNANT, n. Residue; that which is left after the separation, removal or destruction of a part.
ESCAPE, v.i. To flee from and avoid; to get free from danger; to be free or safe from injury.
BLAST, n. A gust or puff of wind; a sudden gust; a violent blowing; a blight.
REJOICE, v.i. To experience joy and gladness in a high degree; to be exhilarated with lively and pleasurable sensations.
corruption_summary: British kingdom in the west Yorkshire hills, Christian while the English around it were heathen, absorbed by Northumbria about 617.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is the shelter of small and shrinking peoples, and he says so in the vocabulary of weather and siege: “thou hast been a strength to the poor, a strength to the needy in his distress, a refuge from the storm, a shadow from the heat” (Isa 25:4). He promises survivors as a matter of his own undertaking: “Yet will I leave a remnant, that ye may have some that shall escape the sword among the nations” (Eze 6:8).

The live temptation for a besieged minority is either despair or a sour triumphalism about the enemy's eventual fall. Habakkuk shows the third way, which costs more than either. He grants the worst case in full, “Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines” (Hab 3:17), and then makes the only move left to a man who has nothing: “Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation” (Hab 3:18). Elmet was absorbed; its Christians were still there afterwards, and so were their churches.

pos: n. (the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of the lower Severn valley, with its see at Worcester)
etymology: Old English Hwicce, a tribal name of uncertain meaning, surviving in Wychwood and Whichford.
biblical_def: The Hwicce held the lower Severn valley and the Cotswold edge, roughly Worcestershire, Gloucestershire and west Warwickshire, and they were a sub-kingdom under Mercian overlordship for most of their history. They were Christianised early by missionaries working up the Severn, and about 680 Theodore of Tarsus divided the vast Mercian diocese and gave the Hwicce a bishop of their own at Worcester, where the see has been ever since; their royal house founded minsters at Gloucester, Bath, Pershore and Evesham and several of its women ruled them as abbesses. The kingdom was absorbed into Mercia in the ninth century, but the diocese of Worcester still follows its boundaries, so that a seventh-century tribal frontier is visible on a modern church map. The dictionary records the Hwicce for the valley and for the figure Scripture draws from well-watered land. The promise given to the obedient is that they shall be like a watered garden, guided continually and satisfied in drought, whose waters do not fail; the fruitfulness is a loan and not a property.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to guide as to lead and direct; to satisfy as to supply fully; a drought as a want of rain; a spring as a fountain of water; and labor as toil and the fruit of toil.
webster_full: GUIDE, v.t. To lead or direct in a way; to conduct in a course or path; to influence; to govern.
SATISFY, v.t. To gratify wants, wishes or desires to the full extent; to supply fully what is desired.
DROUGHT, n. Dryness; want of rain or of water; thirst; want of drink; dryness of the weather.
SPRING, n. A fountain of water; an issue of water from the earth, or the basin of water at its source.
LABOR, n. Exertion of muscular strength, or bodily exertion which occasions weariness; also, the product of toil.
corruption_summary: Severn valley sub-kingdom under Mercia, given its own bishop at Worcester about 680; the diocese still follows its seventh-century bounds.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that fruitfulness is given and kept up by God rather than owned. Isaiah promises guidance and supply together, “thou shalt be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters fail not” (Isa 58:11), and Jeremiah uses the identical figure for a returning people, “and their soul shall be as a watered garden” (Jer 31:12).

The live temptation in a rich valley is to take the richness as a possession and then as a merit. The Psalmist assigns every stage of it to a visitor: “Thou visitest the earth, and waterest it: thou greatly enrichest it with the river of God” (Psa 65:9). What is left to the farmer is work and the blessing of eating what he has worked for: “For thou shalt eat the labour of thine hands: happy shalt thou be, and it shall be well with thee” (Psa 128:2). The minsters of the Hwicce were endowed out of that valley, which makes the point sharper rather than softer.

pos: n. (the south-western Welsh kingdom, the old territory of the Demetae, in which St Davids stands)
etymology: Welsh Dyfed, from the Roman tribal name Demetae, the people of the south-west.
biblical_def: Dyfed was the kingdom of the Welsh south-west, the land of the Demetae, running from the Teifi to the Tywi and out to the sea at St Davids. It kept Christianity unbroken from Roman Britain through the centuries when England was heathen, and its Ogham-inscribed stones, cut in both Irish and Latin letters, show an Irish settlement there and a church literate in two traditions. From Dyfed came David, the chief Welsh saint, whose monastery at Menevia observed a rule of extreme austerity and whose see became the metropolitan claim of the Welsh church against Canterbury; from Dyfed also came the men who taught in the Welsh monastic schools. Giraldus Cambrensis fought his long losing battle for the independence of St Davids in the twelfth century. The dictionary records Dyfed for continuity. A church that was never converted because it was never lost is a rare thing in Britain, and the parable of the two builders explains what makes a house stand through storms: not the absence of rain but the rock it was dug down to.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a rock as a large mass of stony matter; to found as to set or build upon a basis; a flood as a great flow of water; to shake as to cause to totter; and to dig as to open and break the earth.
webster_full: ROCK, n. A large mass of stony matter, usually compounded of two or more simple minerals; defence; means of safety.
FOUND, v.t. To lay the basis of any thing; to set, or place, as on something solid for support.
FLOOD, n. A great flow of water; a body of moving water; an inundation; a deluge.
SHAKE, v.t. To cause to move with quick vibrations; to agitate; to make to totter or tremble.
DIG, v.t. To open and break or turn up the earth with a spade or other sharp instrument.
corruption_summary: The south-western Welsh kingdom of the Demetae, where Christianity continued unbroken from Roman Britain and whose see of St Davids claimed Welsh metropolitan rank.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the test Christ puts on a building, which is obedience: “whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock” (Mat 7:24). The storm is not withheld from that house; it is survived, “and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock” (Mat 7:25).

The live temptation for an old church is to mistake its antiquity for its foundation, and the Welsh metropolitan claim was argued on precisely those grounds for four centuries. Luke adds the detail that makes the difference visible, which is labour out of sight: the wise builder “digged deep, and laid the foundation on a rock” (Luk 6:48). And the city the patriarchs looked for is identified by its architect rather than by its age, “a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Heb 11:10). Continuity is a mercy; it is not a title deed.

pos: n. (the British kingdom of the Lothians, destroyed by the Angles, and the subject of the oldest Welsh poem)
etymology: Welsh Gododdin, from the Roman tribal name Votadini, the people of the Forth shore.
biblical_def: Gododdin was the British kingdom of the Lothians and the Forth shore, the old territory of the Votadini, with strongholds at Traprain Law and on the rock of Edinburgh. It was Christian, being a Romanised British people, and it was destroyed piece by piece as Bernicia expanded north; Edinburgh fell about 638 and the kingdom ended. Its memorial is Y Gododdin, a sequence of elegies attributed to the poet Aneirin and preserved in Welsh, lamenting a war band of some three hundred men who rode from Edinburgh to Catraeth and were killed almost to the last man; it is the oldest surviving poetry in any British language, it mentions the taking of communion before the battle, and it may contain the earliest reference to Arthur. The dictionary records Gododdin for the poem's preservation. A kingdom was wiped out and nothing of its archives, churches or dynasty survives, and the one thing that came through was a set of verses about men who died. Scripture promises that work done in the Lord is not lost, whatever becomes of the people who did it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stedfast as firm and fixed; unmoveable as not to be moved; in vain as to no purpose; to reap as to gather a harvest; and to reward as to repay for service.
webster_full: STEDFAST, a. Fast fixed; firm; firmly fixed or established; constant; resolute; steady.
UNMOVEABLE, a. That cannot be moved from its place; not to be shaken; firm; fixed; steadfast.
VAIN, a. Empty; worthless; having no substance, value or importance; ineffectual; fruitless.
REAP, v.t. To cut grain with a sickle; to gather a harvest; to clear of a crop by reaping; to obtain.
REWARD, v.t. To give in return; to repay; to recompense, either good or evil.
corruption_summary: British kingdom of the Lothians, destroyed by Bernicia about 638, remembered only in Y Gododdin, the oldest surviving poem in a British language.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that labour done for God is not lost with the people who did it. Paul says so to a church in a city that no longer exists, and he gives the reason: “be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58). The Psalmist promises the same of a man rather than a realm, “the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance” (Psa 112:6).

The live temptation is to measure faithfulness by survival, which would condemn Gododdin outright, since it kept nothing at all but a poem about a defeat. Paul warns against the weariness that such reckoning produces: “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9). The word to Asa's generation puts the encouragement in the imperative, with the recompense left to God and the timing unstated: “Be ye strong therefore, and let not your hands be weak: for your work shall be rewarded” (2Ch 15:7).
